source_evidence.observation: The paper defines whatever order of evaluation through rooted binary summation trees with k leaves and k-1 binary internal nodes. Superscripts distinguish perturbation coefficients that may be pairwise distinct, and c is deliberately left unperturbed.

source_evidence.anchor: Equations (1.7)-(1.8) and the paragraph ending with any evaluation order of the sums involved
source_evidence.observation: The underlying result uses rounding to nearest with arbitrary tie-breaking and applies for any radix, dimension, and summation order. Its constants are linear in u, contain no O(u^2) term, and impose no dimension-dependent smallness condition.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.1, Floating-point numbers and rounding to nearest
source_evidence.observation: F is a symmetric set of finite floating-point numbers containing zero, with radix beta >= 2, precision p >= 1, and a finite exponent range. The map fl rounds a real number to a nearest floating-point value, with no prescribed tie-breaking rule.

source_evidence.anchor: Equations (2.1a)-(2.1b) and the surrounding underflow discussion
source_evidence.observation: The unit roundoff is u = (1/2) beta^(1-p), hence u <= 1/2. Underflow means an inexact rounding of a real value in the subnormal range; multiplication and division can underflow or overflow, whereas floating-point addition cannot underflow under this definition.

The summation result used later first rounds each real summand x_i to fl(x_i) and then adds the resulting floating-point numbers in an arbitrary order. Taking x_i to be products of floating-point inputs covers inner products.

For a sum of n real terms with one exactly floating-point term, Theorem 3.1 bounds the residual of a real rho approximating the computed sum. Its quantifier order is inputs and evaluation order first, followed by the residual conclusion.

source_evidence.anchor: Paragraph preceding Corollary 3.2 and the first conclusion of Corollary 3.2
source_evidence.observation: For nonzero b in F and computed y-hat = fl(s-hat/b), the corollary treats rho = b y-hat as an exact real product and proves an absolute residual bound with coefficient n u.

Lemma 4.1 concerns y = (c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i)/b_k for positive k, finite floating-point inputs, and nonzero b_k. Every permitted evaluation order without underflow or overflow admits coefficients satisfying b_k y-hat (1 + theta_k^(0)) = c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i (1 + theta_k^(i)), with absolute coefficient bounds k u. When b_k = 1 and division is omitted, the bounds improve to (k-1)u.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Lemma 4.1, from Assume first that b_k = 1 through the appeal to Corollary 3.2
source_evidence.observation: For b_k = 1 the proof obtains y-hat - y = epsilon (abs(y-hat) + sum abs(a_i b_i)), where abs(epsilon) <= (k-1)u, and explicitly chooses epsilon^(0) = -sign(y-hat) epsilon and epsilon^(i) = -sign(a_i b_i) epsilon. The general nonzero-divisor case is said to follow analogously from Corollary 3.2 with b = b_k, n = k, x_1 = c, and x_{i+1} = -a_i b_i.

binders: Universally quantify k in N_{>0}. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
Universally quantify scalar inputs a_1,...,a_{k-1}, b_1,...,b_{k-1}, b_k, and c in F. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)

For each permitted floating-point evaluation order and its resulting computed value y-hat, existentially choose real coefficients theta_k^(0),...,theta_k^(k-1); the coefficients may depend on the inputs and computation. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 3, anchor: footnote 1.)
hypotheses: The divisor b_k is nonzero. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
The exact real expression is y = (c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i)/b_k, and it is evaluated in floating-point arithmetic. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
No underflow or overflow occurs during the floating-point evaluation. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
The special bound assumes b_k = 1 and that the division is omitted. (PDF p. 10, anchor: sentence beginning If b_k = 1.)
conclusions: General nonzero-divisor conclusion: there exist real coefficients such that b_k y-hat (1 + theta_k^(0)) = c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i (1 + theta_k^(i)) and abs(theta_k^(i)) <= k u for every coefficient occurring in the identity. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)

Unit-divisor conclusion: when b_k = 1 and no division is performed, the same identity holds with abs(theta_k^(i)) <= (k-1)u for every occurring coefficient. (PDF p. 10, anchor: sentence immediately following the Lemma 4.1 display.)

In the explicitly proved unit-divisor case, one common residual scalar epsilon can be used to construct sign-aligned coefficients epsilon^(0) = -sign(y-hat)epsilon and epsilon^(i) = -sign(a_i b_i)epsilon for 1 <= i < k, with magnitude bounded by (k-1)u. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1, sign construction.)

The proof indicates, rather than writes out, the analogous general-case construction obtained from Corollary 3.2 with the exact left quantity b_k y-hat and bound k u. (PDF p. 10, anchor: final sentence of the proof of Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 8, anchor: first conclusion of Corollary 3.2.)
definitions_and_conventions: F denotes finite floating-point values; y is an exact real expression, whereas y-hat is the floating-point result. (PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)

The products a_i b_i and b_k y-hat in the concluding identity are exact real products used in an algebraic backward-error representation, not additional computed multiplications. (PDF p. 8, anchor: paragraph identifying rho as the exact product; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 display.)

The coefficient theta_k^(0) perturbs the aggregate b_k y-hat, while theta_k^(i) perturbs the complete product a_i b_i; the lemma does not separately perturb a_i, b_i, b_k, or y-hat. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
The scalar c remains exactly unperturbed. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion; PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph beginning Note also.)
Whatever order refers to arbitrary rooted binary parenthesizations of the signed summands, not to a fixed recursive order. (PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph beginning Each of the three identities.)
implicit_context: Inherited from Section 2, every elementary rounding uses round-to-nearest in a finite floating-point system, with arbitrary tie-breaking. (PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1.)
The proof formalizes the numerator using n = k, x_1 = c, and x_{i+1} = -a_i b_i for 1 <= i < k. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1.)

Existence of the perturbation coefficients follows from converting an absolute residual bound into an exact algebraic identity; uniqueness is neither claimed nor needed. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1.)
There is no restriction on k beyond positivity, even when k u >= 1. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Section 4.1 opening paragraph.)
statement.algorithm_linkage: The numerator is modeled as the floating-point summation of the k signed leaves c and -a_i b_i in any rooted binary order; for general b_k, the resulting computed numerator is then divided by b_k and rounded, while the b_k = 1 variant omits that division. This linkage is explicit through x_1 = c and x_{i+1} = -a_i b_i in the proof and through the paper's binary-tree definition of evaluation order. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph defining whatever order of evaluation.)
numerical_model: F is a finite, symmetric floating-point set containing zero, with radix beta >= 2, precision p >= 1, and a finite exponent range. (PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1 first paragraph.)
The rounding map fl selects a nearest floating-point value, with no fixed tie-breaking rule. (PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1 definition of fl.)
The unit roundoff is u = (1/2) beta^(1-p), with u <= 1/2. (PDF p. 5, anchor: equations (2.1a)-(2.1b) and following sentence.)

The result applies for arbitrary radix, tie-breaking rule, dimension, and summation order, subject to the exceptional-value assumptions. (PDF p. 4, anchor: paragraph ending any evaluation order of the sums involved.)
error_notions: The conclusion is a componentwise backward-error representation: each complete product term and the aggregate computed-side term receive a multiplicative real perturbation. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)

The perturbation size is measured by scalar absolute values abs(theta_k^(i)); no relative forward-error bound for y-hat versus y is asserted by the lemma. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
The absolute residual estimate in the proof is auxiliary and is converted into the exact backward identity by sign-aligned coefficients. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1.)
norms: Only ordinary scalar absolute value is used; Lemma 4.1 contains no vector, matrix, or operator norm. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 and its proof.)
constants_and_indexing: The numerator contains k-1 product terms indexed by i = 1,...,k-1, plus the unperturbed term c, for k total summation leaves. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 3, anchor: binary-tree description.)

The computed-side coefficient has superscript 0, and product coefficients have superscripts 1,...,k-1; the natural range of the phrase for all i is therefore i in {0,...,k-1}. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
The general constant is exactly k u; omitting division when b_k = 1 reduces it by one unit roundoff to exactly (k-1)u. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 and following sentence.)

For k = 1, the indexed product sum is empty by the displayed indexing, leaving y = c/b_1; in the b_1 = 1 no-division case the stated coefficient bound is zero. This edge case is inferred from k in N_{>0} and the range 1 <= i < k rather than discussed separately. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
higher_order_terms: The bounds are the literal linear quantities k u and (k-1)u, with no gamma factor, omitted O(u^2) term, or condition such as k u < 1. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Section 4.1 opening paragraph and Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 4, anchor: discussion following equation (1.8).)
The displayed backward relation is an exact algebraic identity, not an equality modulo higher-order terms. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
exceptional_values: All inputs belong to the finite set F, so infinities and NaNs are outside the stated input domain. (PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1 first paragraph; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 binders.)
Division by zero is excluded by the explicit hypothesis b_k != 0. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)

Underflow and overflow must be absent throughout the evaluated operations; multiplication and division can trigger either event, and additions can overflow but cannot underflow under the paper's definition. (PDF p. 5, anchor: underflow and operation discussion; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
Zero values of y-hat or individual products are not excluded by the lemma. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 hypotheses.)

undebatable_constraints: The exact expression has the division outside the entire numerator: y = (c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i)/b_k. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
The divisor is a nonzero finite floating-point number, and every a_i, b_i, and c is also in F. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
The conclusion must preserve both coefficient families, including theta_k^(0) on b_k y-hat and theta_k^(i) on every product term. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
The scalar c is not perturbed. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
The general bound is k u; the improved (k-1)u bound applies specifically to b_k = 1 with no division. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 and its immediately following sentence.)

The claim covers every summation order represented by a binary summation tree, provided no underflow or overflow occurs. (PDF p. 3, anchor: definition of whatever order; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)
The constants contain no higher-order remainder and require no smallness assumption on k u. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Section 4.1 opening paragraph.)

The left product b_k y-hat in the backward identity is exact rather than a further rounded operation. (PDF p. 8, anchor: paragraph identifying rho as an exact product; PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 display.)

ambiguities.issue: The paper does not define sign(0) in the inspected context.
ambiguities.evidence: The unit-case construction uses sign(y-hat) and sign(a_i b_i) and then states equal coefficient magnitudes, while zero values are not excluded. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1, sign construction.)
ambiguities.impact: With the common convention sign(0) = 0, the displayed equality abs(epsilon^(i)) = abs(epsilon) need not hold for a zero-associated coefficient. The backward identity and upper bound remain obtainable by assigning coefficients on zero terms arbitrarily within the bound, but a formalization should not silently rely on an unstated zero-sign convention.

ambiguities.issue: The exact index set in the phrase for all i is implicit.
ambiguities.evidence: The display contains theta_k^(0) on the left and theta_k^(i) for i = 1,...,k-1 on the right, followed only by for all i. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 displayed conclusion.)
ambiguities.impact: The evident intended range is {0,...,k-1}; formalizing only the summation range 1,...,k-1 would incorrectly omit the bound on theta_k^(0).

ambiguities.issue: The general nonzero-divisor proof does not write the sign-aligned witness coefficients explicitly.
ambiguities.evidence: After giving explicit formulas only for b_k = 1, the proof says the general case is handled analogously using Corollary 3.2. (PDF p. 10, anchor: final sentence of the proof of Lemma 4.1.)
ambiguities.impact: The lemma's general-case identity and k u bounds are explicit, but the stronger assertion that one common residual scalar yields equal-magnitude sign-aligned coefficients in that case is an inference from analogous reasoning, not a separately stated conclusion.

ambiguities.issue: Fused multiply-add evaluation is not discussed.
ambiguities.evidence: The proof maps product terms to separate real summands x_{i+1} = -a_i b_i and relies on a model that rounds each x_i before summation. (PDF p. 10, anchor: proof of Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 6, anchor: equation (2.4) and following paragraph.)
ambiguities.impact: The source contract directly covers the separately rounded product-and-sum model used in the proof. Coverage of an implementation that fuses multiplication and addition would require an additional argument.

contract_plain_english: For every positive k and finite floating-point inputs a_i, b_i, b_k, and c with b_k nonzero, compute (c - sum a_i b_i)/b_k using round-to-nearest floating-point arithmetic, allowing any binary parenthesization of the numerator and assuming no underflow or overflow. The resulting y-hat admits an exact backward interpretation in which c remains unchanged, the exact aggregate b_k y-hat is multiplied by 1 + theta_k^(0), and each exact product a_i b_i is multiplied by 1 + theta_k^(i). Every such coefficient is bounded in absolute value by k u. If b_k = 1 and division is omitted, every bound improves to (k-1)u. The unit-divisor proof explicitly constructs the coefficients from one residual scalar with signs opposite to y-hat and the product terms. These are exact, O(u^2)-free constants with no restriction on k. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1 and its proof; PDF p. 3, anchor: evaluation-order convention; PDF p. 5, anchor: Section 2.1 rounding model.)
